# ADR-0001 — Git as the source of truth for network and platform configuration

## Context

The engagement needs backup, restore, drift detection and compliance across heterogeneous domains, with evidence usable for accreditation. Configuration state was previously held in tools and in operators' heads.

## Options considered

**Commercial orchestrator with an internal configuration database.** Mature, transactional, vendor-supported; costly, opinionated, and the state lives inside a product.

**Configuration backup tooling only.** Cheap and quick; gives history but no intended state, therefore no real drift or compliance.

**Git as the intended state, with an inventory product alongside.** Reviewable, reproducible, tool-agnostic; requires building the pipeline.

## Decision

Git holds the intended configuration, templates, fallback plans and rules. An inventory product holds assets and per-device data. Nothing reaches a managed system except through the validated pipeline.

## Consequences

Change review becomes mandatory rather than cultural. Rollback is a revert. Undocumented manual changes appear as drift, which is intended. The team must learn a pipeline discipline that did not previously exist.

## Revisit when

A vendor offers an orchestrator whose state can itself be driven from Git without duplication.

# ADR-0002 — Network source of truth and compliance engine

## Context

An inventory of record is needed to drive automation, feed the configuration database, and support drift and compliance reporting across three domains.

## Options considered

**Commercial orchestrator suite.** Strong native modelling, transactional configuration; licence cost and lock-in on the state.

**Inventory product with a configuration compliance extension.** Open source, active ecosystem, native backup / intended / compliance workflow, extensible jobs and buttons; requires assembling the transport layer.

**Spreadsheet plus scripts.** Zero licence, unbounded maintenance cost, no compliance story.

## Decision

An open-source inventory product extended with a configuration compliance module is the network source of truth and the drift and compliance engine.

## Consequences

The compliance workflow is obtained rather than built. Population of the inventory becomes the critical path item of the foundation work package, and is routinely underestimated by a factor of two.

## Revisit when

Inventory ownership moves to the service management platform's network inventory product and can drive automation directly.

# ADR-0003 — Orchestration and approval engine

## Context

Operators are not developers. They need buttons, forms and role-scoped access, and every production action must carry a recorded human approval.

## Options considered

**Command-line playbooks only.** No cost; unusable by first-line operators, no approval trail.

**Lightweight job runner.** Simple to operate, gives buttons and forms; no native approval node, weaker role model.

**Full orchestration platform with workflow approval nodes.** Buttons, surveys, fine-grained roles, approval nodes with timeout and notification, API-drivable; heavier to operate.

## Decision

A full orchestration platform is used, with workflow approval nodes as the mandatory gate for production actions.

## Consequences

Approval, notification and audit are obtained natively rather than built. Role modelling becomes an explicit design task. The platform is one more component to operate on the management cluster.

## Revisit when

The service management platform's own approval workflow can gate execution directly without losing the operator-facing buttons.

# ADR-0004 — Event-driven remediation engine

## Context

Alarms must be mapped to candidate remediation workflows, with deduplication and storm protection, without giving the alerting system a write path to the network.

## Options considered

**Alerting webhooks calling playbooks directly.** Fewest components; no deduplication, no locking, no shadow mode, and the alerting system becomes an actor.

**General-purpose event automation platform.** Very capable, mature; another ecosystem to learn and operate.

**Rulebook engine from the same automation ecosystem as the orchestrator.** Native fit with the orchestration platform, declarative rules, supports a log-only mode.

## Decision

A rulebook engine from the same ecosystem as the orchestration platform maps qualified alarms to workflows, and never executes actions itself: it launches a workflow whose first node is an approval.

## Consequences

One ecosystem, one skill set. Shadow mode is available for rule validation. The mapping layer becomes an asset to version and promote like code.

## Revisit when

Correlation moves into the service management platform, which would make the rulebook engine a pass-through worth reconsidering.

# ADR-0005 — Access the mobile core exclusively through the element manager northbound interfaces

## Context

The mobile core runs on dedicated vendor-operated infrastructure with its own element manager, which maintains its own view of node configuration. Direct node access over standard protocols is technically conceivable.

## Options considered

**Direct configuration of nodes.** Uniform with the transport domain, no dependency on element manager interfaces; creates a second configuration master, triggers resynchronizations, and voids supportability.

**Element manager northbound interfaces only.** Preserves supportability and single mastership; capability depends on version and licensing, and must be audited before commitment.

## Decision

All configuration operations on the core pass through the element manager northbound interfaces. Nothing is deployed on the vendor platform.

## Consequences

Backup becomes an export, drift a comparison of exports, a fallback plan a pre-validated delta. Observability of the core is limited to what the vendor exports, and any gap must be declared. The feasibility of the whole core scope depends on an audit performed before commitment.

## Revisit when

The vendor exposes a supported model-driven interface with equivalent guarantees, or the audit shows the northbound interfaces cannot export, import or read.

# ADR-0006 — GitOps engine for the container platform

## Context

The container platform hosts the mission-critical application suite and the other services. A continuous reconciliation engine is required, and the platform vendor ships one.

## Options considered

**Application-centric GitOps engine.** Excellent application-oriented user experience, large community; a second control plane alongside the platform's own.

**The platform's native multi-cluster GitOps engine.** One control plane, aligned with platform support and lifecycle, well suited to a fleet of clusters; less application-centric tooling.

## Decision

The platform's native GitOps engine is used, and it is the only reconciliation engine for that domain.

## Consequences

One control plane and one support path. Workload drift is detected natively. Cluster definitions and node operating system configuration remain outside its scope and must be covered by the automation chain — a distinct engineering item that is easy to overlook.

## Revisit when

The team standardizes on the application-centric engine for other reasons; running both remains excluded.

# ADR-0007 — Dedicated management cluster with its own storage and southbound paths

## Context

The automation chain, the analytics and the collection tier must run somewhere. The simplest option is to place them on an existing workload cluster.

## Options considered

**Co-hosting on a workload cluster.** Cheapest; the recovery tooling shares a failure domain with what it recovers.

**Dedicated management cluster with its own storage and its own paths to the element manager and the network devices.** Additional footprint; removes the circular dependency and allows an independent break-glass path.

## Decision

A dedicated management cluster is used, and a documented, drilled break-glass procedure exists for its own unavailability.

## Consequences

Additional cluster footprint and lifecycle. In exchange, an incident on the workload clusters cannot disable the chain that repairs them. The break-glass export becomes a deliverable to maintain and to exercise.

## Revisit when

The platform offers a supported control-plane isolation model that provides the same guarantee at lower footprint.

# ADR-0008 — Split observability: service plane and infrastructure plane

## Context

Two capable products are in the landscape: a search and analytics platform already used for service signals, and the container platform vendor's topology-centric observability product. Both ingest open telemetry and both can alert.

## Options considered

**Single analytics platform for everything.** One product to operate and licence; loses topology and health-model experience for the platform, and the vendor's platform observability extensions.

**Single platform observability product for everything.** Loses long audit retention, free-text investigation, field-level security and the replay capability the shadow validation depends on.

**Both, split by nature of signal.** Each product does what it is best at; requires an explicit boundary and a bridge to keep correlation single-engine.

## Decision

Signals contributing to a delivered service go to the analytics platform; signals describing the hosting platform go to the vendor observability product. A single collection layer routes on signal attributes, and the infrastructure plane forwards health events into the service plane so that correlation and closed-loop triggering remain performed by one engine.

## Consequences

Two products to operate and licence. Clear audience separation. No source is instrumented twice. The bridge between planes becomes a design item that must not be forgotten, or the split fragments diagnosis.

## Revisit when

The platform observability product is not in the contractual scope, in which case a single analytics platform with index and role separation is preferred.

# ADR-0009 — Mastership arbitration between inventory systems

## Context

Three systems legitimately claim to hold inventory: the network source of truth driving automation, the service management platform's network inventory, and the configuration management database.

## Options considered

**Network inventory product as master, automation reading from it.** Aligns with the service management strategy; unproven as a driver for automation inventory, and dependent on release capability.

**Network source of truth as master for automation-facing data, one-way sync outward.** Immediately workable; leaves the service model to the inventory product.

**Bidirectional synchronization.** Superficially attractive, produces irreconcilable records.

## Decision

For the first phase, the network source of truth masters device and cluster data used by automation; the network inventory product masters the service and resource model; the configuration management database masters configuration items. Synchronization is one-directional per attribute.

## Consequences

No circular synchronization. The arbitration must be validated with the platform owner during framing, and is expected to be revisited once the inventory product is in service. This is currently the least verified decision in the set.

## Revisit when

The network inventory product demonstrates it can drive automation inventory directly at the required fidelity.

# ADR-0010 — Inference served by an external endpoint

## Context

No local acceleration hardware was available. The assistant layer needs a reasoning model, and the vendor supports external providers.

## Options considered

**External provider with contractual and technical controls.** No hardware investment, best latency and quality; tool outputs may carry configuration fragments, addresses and credentials outside the trust boundary.

**Defer the assistant layer.** No exposure; loses the benefit.

**Local inference on general-purpose processors.** Keeps everything inside the boundary; degraded latency.

## Decision

Use an external inference endpoint with scope restriction, redaction and contracted data-protection terms.

## Consequences

Confidentiality becomes a procedural control that must be proven repeatedly to an accreditation authority. Superseded shortly after being taken, once the security trade-off was re-examined.

## Revisit when

Superseded — see ADR-0011.

# ADR-0011 — Inference served locally on general-purpose processors

## Context

Re-examination of ADR-0010 concluded that sending configuration fragments, addresses and potentially credential material to an external provider is not defensible for an accredited mission-critical system, even with redaction controls.

## Options considered

**Keep the external endpoint with stronger controls.** Best latency; the control remains procedural and must be re-proven at every audit.

**Local inference on general-purpose processors with a small model.** Structural confidentiality, compatible with a disconnected deployment; response times of tens of seconds to minutes, and reduced tool-calling reliability with smaller models.

**Defer until acceleration hardware is funded.** Zero risk, zero benefit.

## Decision

Inference is served locally on a dedicated node pool, starting on general-purpose processors with a small model. The endpoint is a configuration value so that acceleration hardware can be added later without redesign.

## Consequences

Confidentiality becomes structural rather than contractual. Capacity replaces confidentiality as the limiting factor, so latency and answer quality must be measured before opening the production profile. Read-only tooling keeps model errors informational rather than operational.

## Revisit when

Acceleration hardware becomes available, or measurement shows latency is unacceptable even for engineering use.

# ADR-0012 — Shadow environment on a separate cluster

## Context

Rules must be validated against real traffic, which means the validation environment receives production data and could, if misconfigured, act on production.

## Options considered

**Namespace separation inside an existing cluster.** Cheap; isolation rests on configuration discipline and is hard to demonstrate to an auditor.

**Separate cluster with no production credentials and no route to production assets.** Additional footprint; isolation becomes a structural property.

## Decision

The shadow environment runs on a separate cluster holding no production credentials and having no network route to production assets. Its most dangerous possible action is writing a log line.

## Consequences

Additional cluster to operate. Isolation is demonstrable rather than asserted, which matters for accreditation. The traffic duplication queue is explicitly allowed to drop data rather than exert back-pressure on production collection.

## Revisit when

Platform-level isolation guarantees become strong enough to make separate clusters unnecessary.

# ADR-0013 — Subscriber and SIM provisioning excluded from the configuration chain

## Context

The service management platform's network inventory can model subscriber identity modules as resources, which raised the question of whether their lifecycle belongs in the configuration management perimeter.

## Options considered

**Include provisioning in the configuration chain.** One chain for everything; mixes a subscriber data flow with a system configuration flow, with different controls, different audit needs and different failure modes.

**Keep provisioning as a separate flow.** Clear separation of concerns; requires an explicit integration to specify and budget.

## Decision

Inventory and ordering workflow stay with the service management platform; profile generation, download and activation stay with the certified provisioning platform and the subscriber database. The configuration chain does not participate.

## Consequences

The integration between the ordering workflow and the provisioning platform must be specified and costed rather than assumed available. Out-of-the-box coverage claims must be verified against the exact purchased release.

## Revisit when

A vendor demonstrates an integrated capability covering both, with controls acceptable for subscriber data.

# ADR-0014 — Normalized Envelope Response and Unified Server Configuration for MCP

## Context

Third-party MCP client integrations (such as Claude Desktop, Cursor, and automated pipelines) require deterministic error handling, structured status codes, and consistent payload structures across all tools. Without a standard contract, raw exceptions and internal database errors leak into client interfaces, while configuration drift between multiple settings classes creates deployment ambiguities.

## Options considered

**Ad-hoc responses with raw exceptions.**
Returning bare dictionaries on success and raising raw Python exceptions on failure. Quick to code initially, but leaks internal container paths, SQL/Cypher parsing errors, and forces every client to parse arbitrary error messages.

**Normalized response envelope and typed configuration.**
Wrapping every tool response in a standard envelope schema (`status`, `data`, `error`, `code`) with typed helpers (`ok_response`, `error_response`, `not_found_response`, `invalid_argument_response`) and centralizing configuration in a single typed `ServerConfig` model with strict environment parsing.

## Decision

Adopt the normalized envelope schema (`mcp_server/core/envelope.py`) across all MCP endpoints and unify server configuration under `ServerConfig` (`mcp_server/core/config.py`). All tools return envelope dictionaries, and internal errors are mapped to normalized codes.

## Consequences

External MCP clients and web frontends have a predictable contract. Stack traces and database internals are shielded from clients. Adding or modifying tools requires adhering to the envelope protocol.

## Revisit when

An official MCP protocol specification introduces a mandatory native envelope or structured error standard superseding Starlette HTTP/JSON envelopes.

# ADR-0015 — Dual-Plane Physical Database Isolation (Knowledge vs Engagement)

## Context

LLMOps serves two distinct domains with radically different operational and security profiles:
1. **Knowledge Plane**: Global, reusable, non-confidential architectural knowledge (principles, frameworks, controls, patterns, skills, zero-draft templates).
2. **Engagement Plane**: Highly confidential, project-specific client data (stakeholder verbatim, interview statements, maturity boards, trade-off conflicts, and arbitration cards).

Mixing these two domains in a single shared database creates grave confidentiality risks: a flaw in a Cypher query or a misconfigured multi-tenant filter could leak client project data into public demo queries or cross-client sessions.

## Options considered

**Logical multi-tenancy in a single shared database.**
All nodes (Assets, Frameworks, Statements, Conflicts) reside in one database file with an `engagement_id` property. High operational simplicity, but zero defense-in-depth: any unfiltered `MATCH (n) RETURN n` or Cypher injection leaks confidential client engagements.

**Strict dual-plane physical database isolation.**
Physically isolate the Knowledge Base into `data/knowledge.lbug` and each client engagement into dedicated files `data/engagements/<engagement-id>.lbug`. Enforce separate database handles via a connection router (`open_connection`) and strictly prohibit cross-database Cypher joins.

## Decision

Enforce strict dual-plane physical database isolation. The Knowledge Plane is completely decoupled from Engagement databases. Cross-plane Cypher joins are physically impossible at the storage layer. Authorization choke point (`authorise()`) verifies tenant scoping before resolving any engagement file path.

## Consequences

Client confidentiality is guaranteed at the filesystem level. The Knowledge Plane can be mounted and served read-only on public demo instances (`LLMOPS_PLANE=knowledge` or scoped demo) without any possibility of client data exposure. Engagement tools require explicit engagement scope routing.

## Revisit when

A distributed graph database with hardware-enforced cryptographic tenant isolation and verified zero-leakage cross-database federation becomes a core platform dependency.

# ADR-0016 — HSM mandatory for 5G NAS credentials and MCX key material

## Status

**Active** — applies to all mission-critical mobile network engagements at national scale.

## Context

A national mission-critical mobile network handles long-term subscriber credentials (SUPI/SUCI), MCX group and individual key material (KMS, 3GPP TS 33.179), and PKI root CA private keys. These assets are the trust anchors of the entire system: compromise of any one of them enables impersonation of subscribers, decryption of emergency communications, or forgery of certificates.

Software-only key stores (file-based, database-backed, or TPM-only) are insufficient for this threat model because:
- A compromised container runtime or hypervisor can exfiltrate software-resident keys.
- A rogue administrator with access to the key store host can extract key material without triggering audit events visible to the SOC.
- Regulatory frameworks (NIS2, SecNumCloud, 3GPP TS 33.501 §6.1) either mandate or strongly recommend hardware-backed key operations for nationally critical systems.

## Decision

**Hardware Security Modules (HSM), certified at Common Criteria EAL4+ or equivalent, are mandatory for the following operations in any national mission-critical mobile network:**

| HSM Use Case | Protected Operation | Normative Basis |
|---|---|---|
| 5G NAS — SUPI/SUCI protection | Long-term subscriber key (K), SUPI concealment, AUSF key derivation | 3GPP TS 33.501 §6.1 |
| 5G NAS — Authentication | AUSF/UDM authentication procedures | 3GPP TS 33.501 |
| PKI root CA | Root and offline issuing CA private key generation, storage, signing | Industry best practice, SecNumCloud |
| MCX KMS | Group identity key (GIK), client key material signing (3GPP TS 33.179) | 3GPP TS 33.179 §7 |
| Secrets vault master key | Unsealing key for the secrets management system | Defense-in-depth |

No software-only implementation of any of the above is acceptable for a system at national scale. A documented exception with formal risk acceptance by the client CISO and programme security authority is required before any deviation.

## Consequences

**Positive:**
- Cryptographic operations on subscriber credentials are hardware-bound; key material never appears in plaintext outside the HSM boundary.
- A compromised orchestration layer, hypervisor, or administrator account cannot exfiltrate long-term key material.
- HSM audit logs provide tamper-evident evidence for security investigations (`ADR-0008`).
- Compliance with 3GPP TS 33.501, NIS2 Art. 21(2)(h), and SecNumCloud requirements is structurally guaranteed.

**Negative:**
- HSMs introduce a latency overhead for key operations (typically 1–5 ms per operation) — this is acceptable for authentication flows but must be factored into the MCPTT access time budget (`PAT-011`).
- HSM provisioning, clustering, and backup/restore procedures add operational complexity. The break-glass procedure for HSM failure must be defined before go-live.
- CC EAL4+ certified HSMs from approved vendors (e.g., Thales Luna, Utimaco, Entrust) have lead times of 8–16 weeks — procurement must begin at programme start.

## Compliance

| Framework | Article / Clause | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| 3GPP TS 33.501 | §6.1, §6.2 | Long-term credentials shall be protected with at least USIM-level security; operator AUSF/UDM key protection is recommended to be hardware-backed |
| NIS2 Directive | Art. 21(2)(h) | Cryptography and encryption measures commensurate with risk |
| SecNumCloud | REQ-CRYPTO-03 | HSM required for root CA and subscriber credential operations in qualified cloud services |
| ISO/IEC 27001 | A.8.24 | Use of cryptography — key management lifecycle including hardware protection |

# P-001 — Generalized GitOps

## Statement

Intended configurations, fallback plans, triggering rules, correlation rules and automation code are versioned in Git. Every change goes through review and a validation pipeline before it can reach a managed system.

## Why

A managed system with more than one entry path cannot be reasoned about. Versioning is not primarily about rollback; it is about making every change reviewable, attributable and reproducible, which is what an accreditation authority asks for.

## Implications

- The pipeline, not an operator, is the only writer.
- Rollback becomes a revert plus a redeploy rather than a separate procedure.
- Anything not in Git does not exist: undocumented manual changes appear as drift, which is the intended behaviour.

## How to verify

Attempt a manual change on a managed asset outside the pipeline; it must surface in the next drift report.

# P-002 — Human in the loop

## Statement

Detection is automatic, decision is human, execution is automated. No remediation action reaches production without an explicit human approval, recorded in the service management system.

## Why

The failure mode of autonomous remediation is not a wrong action; it is a wrong action taken confidently during an incident, when nobody is watching the automation because everybody is watching the outage.

## Implications

- Every remediation workflow starts with an approval node carrying full context.
- Approval can be delegated to the ITSM change process so it lands in the customer's own governance.
- Autonomy is granted later, per class of event, never as a design default (see P-004).

## How to verify

Trace any production change back to an approval record with an actor and a timestamp. A change without one is a defect.

# P-003 — Bounded unitary actions

## Statement

Closed loops execute simple, idempotent playbooks acting on a single asset, with a known blast radius, pre-checks and post-checks. On failure they stop cleanly and escalate; they never attempt compensation.

## Why

Multi-domain orchestration with error compensation is an order of magnitude more complex to build and to certify than unitary action, and its failure modes are the ones nobody rehearses. A playbook that fails cleanly and escalates is worth more than one that tries to be clever.

## Implications

- No cross-asset transactions in the closed loop.
- Error handling is a two-branch tree: success then post-check, or stop and escalate.
- Complex recovery remains a human-driven runbook, possibly assisted.

## How to verify

Review each remediation playbook: it must touch one asset, be re-runnable without side effects, and have no recovery branch.

# P-004 — Graduated autonomy

## Statement

Moving an action from supervised to automatic approval is a decision taken per class of event, on measured evidence gathered in shadow mode and during a probation period. It is never a design default.

## Why

Autonomy is earned by evidence, not granted by architecture. Tying it to measured false-positive rates makes the trajectory defensible to an accreditation authority and reversible if behaviour degrades.

## Implications

- Each event class carries its autonomy level and the evidence that justified it.
- Low blast-radius, frequently exercised actions graduate first.
- Heavy actions such as a full configuration restore stay permanently gated.

## How to verify

For every automatic action, produce the shadow-mode metrics and the probation record that justified promotion.

# P-005 — Shadow validation before arming

## Statement

Every rule, model or component upgrade is validated on real data before being armed: replayed history for coverage of known incidents, then live duplicated traffic in an isolated environment that can only log what it would have done.

## Why

Pre-production never reproduces the noise, the bursts and the edge cases of a real network. A rule validated only against synthetic traffic is untested where it matters.

## Implications

- An isolated environment with no production credentials and no route to production assets.
- Duplication is temporary, filtered and traced as a versioned configuration change.
- Promotion is a reviewed change against quantified exit criteria.

## How to verify

Verify the shadow environment has no credential and no network path to production; the check is repeated after every infrastructure change.

# P-006 — One chain, several southbound methods

## Statement

A single orchestration, approval, audit and observability layer drives heterogeneous domains. Domain specificities are isolated in a connector layer.

## Why

The value of the chain is in its governance layer, not in its transport. Isolating transport keeps one audit trail and one approval model across domains that have nothing technically in common.

## Implications

- Adding a domain means adding a connector, not a parallel chain.
- The approval, logging and inventory model must not vary by domain.

# P-007 — Respect the vendor boundary

## Statement

Where a vendor element manager owns the configuration of its domain, automation orchestrates above it through official northbound interfaces, never in its place, and deploys nothing on the vendor platform.

## Why

Bypassing an element manager creates two configuration masters, triggers unwanted resynchronizations and voids supportability. The apparent shortcut costs more than the interface it avoids.

## Implications

- Backup becomes an export, drift becomes a comparison of exports, a fallback plan becomes a pre-validated delta.
- Observability of that domain is limited to what the vendor exports; the gap is declared rather than discovered.

## How to verify

Check that no credential exists for direct node access, and that no third-party component is installed on the vendor platform.

# P-009 — Independent failure domain

## Statement

The chain that restores service does not share cluster, storage or network path with the services it restores, and a break-glass procedure exists for its own unavailability.

## Why

The classic embarrassment of automated operations is the recovery tooling being unavailable during the incident it was built for.

## Implications

- Dedicated management cluster with its own storage and southbound paths.
- Critical fallback plans exported to a location reachable without the platform, refreshed by the same pipeline.
- At least two operators trained and periodically drilled.

## How to verify

## Statement

Each data domain has exactly one writing system; every other system holds a read-only copy. Synchronization is one-directional per attribute, not per system.

Two products both claiming to be the source of truth produce circular synchronizations and irreconcilable records, and the reconciliation cost is paid forever.

- Where a product offers overlapping capability, the boundary is agreed with the vendor before integration starts.

# P-011 — Separate observation planes, single collection layer

## Statement

Signals are separated by nature — those contributing to a delivered service, and those describing the platform hosting it — but collected once and routed by attribute.

## Why

Separating audiences and retention needs is legitimate; instrumenting a source twice is not. Routing at the gateway keeps the split from becoming duplication.

## Implications

- One agent fleet, one gateway tier, several backends.
- Adding or replacing a backend is a gateway configuration change, not a redeployment.
- Cross-plane correlation is preserved by forwarding platform events into the service plane.

## How to verify

Check that no source sends to two backends and that a platform incident affecting a service is correlated automatically.

# PAT-001 — Supervised closed loop

## Problem

An alarm indicates a condition with a known remediation, but automatic execution is unacceptable because a wrong action during an incident compounds the outage.

## Forces

- Remediation must be fast enough to matter.
- The action must be auditable and attributable.
- Operators are not developers and will not read code at three in the morning.
- Nobody will trust automation they have never seen behave.

## Solution

Alarm to rule engine, which deduplicates, checks the global switch and the per-asset lock, opens the incident, then launches a workflow whose first node is an approval carrying full context: alarm, asset, proposed action, freshness of the plan, latest compliance status. On approval, pre-checks, unitary action, post-checks, incident update. On any failure, stop, restore, escalate.

## Trade-offs

Adds human latency to remediation, which is the point. Requires the approval surface to be usable on a phone at night. Produces a complete audit trail as a by-product.

## When not to use this

Where the action is genuinely reversible, high frequency and low blast radius — restarting a stateless pod, for instance. There, supervision is friction without value; use it only until the behaviour is characterized, then graduate the class under P-004.

## Seen in

One mission-critical mobile network engagement (2026), across transport, container platform and vendor-managed core.

# PAT-002 — Shadow validation of rules

## Problem

A detection rule cannot be trusted until it has met real traffic, but arming it in production to find out is exactly the risk being avoided.

## Forces

- Pre-production traffic never reproduces real noise, bursts or edge cases.
- Rule quality is measurable, but only against reality.
- A validation environment fed with production data is itself a risk if it can act.

## Solution

Two layers. Batch: replay stored alarm history against the candidate rule to measure coverage of known incidents. Real-time: deploy the rule in an isolated environment fed by a temporary, filtered and pseudonymized duplicate of production traffic, where the rule can only record what it would have triggered. Promote by reviewed change against quantified exit criteria.

## Trade-offs

Requires an isolated environment and a duplication path. Delays arming by the length of the observation window. In exchange, false-positive rates are known before anyone is woken up by them.

## When not to use this

For rules whose only effect is to raise a low-priority ticket, the cost of the apparatus exceeds the risk. Deploy those directly in report-only mode instead.

## Seen in

One mission-critical mobile network engagement (2026), across transport, container platform and vendor-managed core.

# PAT-003 — Fallback plan bound to its baseline

## Problem

Pre-validated recovery configurations silently expire when the configuration they assume evolves, and the expiry is discovered during the incident they were prepared for.

## Forces

- Recovery configurations must be prepared in advance to be useful.
- The system they target keeps changing, if only through software upgrades.
- Nobody re-validates a plan spontaneously.

## Solution

Version each plan with an explicit reference to the baseline configuration and the software version it assumes. The validation pipeline blocks, or at minimum raises a blocking alert on, any baseline change that is not accompanied by revalidation of the dependent plans. A periodic report lists plans and their freshness, and the critical subset is exported for the break-glass path by the same pipeline.

## Trade-offs

Adds a constraint to every baseline change. Makes plan debt visible, which is uncomfortable and useful.

## When not to use this

Where recovery is generic and configuration-independent — restoring the last known-good state, for instance — the binding adds ceremony without protection.

One mission-critical mobile network engagement (2026), across transport, container platform and vendor-managed core.

# PAT-004 — Break-glass with an independent failure domain

## Problem

The tooling built to restore service is unavailable during the incident it was built for, because it shares infrastructure with what failed.

## Forces

- Automation concentrates capability, therefore concentrates risk.
- Operators lose the manual skill the automation replaced.
- The failure is discovered exactly when it cannot be fixed.

## Solution

Run the chain on a dedicated cluster with its own storage and its own southbound paths. Export the critical recovery configurations, in executable form, to a location reachable without the platform, refreshed by the same pipeline that validates them. Train at least two operators and drill the procedure periodically.

## Trade-offs

Additional footprint and a procedure to maintain. The drill costs a half-day per period and is the only thing that proves the arrangement works.

## When not to use this

For systems where a prolonged outage is commercially unpleasant but not dangerous, the drill cadence can be relaxed — but the independence of the failure domain should not be.

# PAT-005 — Two observation planes, one collection layer

## Problem

Service assurance and platform operations need different tools, different retention and different audiences, but instrumenting every source twice is wasteful and produces divergent truths.

## Forces

- Audit retention on service signals is long; platform retention is operational.
- Platform teams and network operations teams want different products.
- Correlation must not be fragmented by the split.

## Solution

Collect once. Route at the gateway on signal attributes towards the two backends. Forward health and alert events from the infrastructure plane into the service plane so that correlation and closed-loop triggering remain performed by a single engine. Adding or replacing a backend becomes a gateway configuration change.

## Trade-offs

Two backends to operate and licence. Requires discipline in attribute tagging at the source, otherwise routing degrades into duplication.

## When not to use this

Where one team operates both service and platform, and retention needs are similar, a single backend with index and role separation is simpler and should be preferred.

# PAT-006 — Vendor boundary through the northbound interface

## Problem

A vendor element manager owns the configuration of its domain, but the automation chain needs backup, drift detection and recovery actions there.

## Forces

- Bypassing the element manager voids supportability and creates a second master.
- Northbound capability varies by version and licensing and is often overstated.
- The domain still has to be covered by the same governance as the rest.

## Solution

Treat the vendor domain as an appliance with an interface. Backup is an export, drift is a comparison of exports, a fallback plan is a pre-validated delta applied through the interface. Audit the actual interface capabilities before committing scope, using a structured questionnaire, and declare any observability gap rather than discovering it.

## Trade-offs

Automation fidelity is capped by what the vendor exposes. In exchange, supportability is preserved and the configuration has a single master.

## When not to use this

Where the vendor supports and documents direct model-driven access with equivalent guarantees, the indirection adds latency for no benefit.

## Seen in

One mission-critical mobile network engagement (2026), across transport, container platform and vendor-managed core.

# PAT-007 — Advisory assistant with prepare-only tooling

## Problem

A reasoning assistant would materially help diagnosis, but giving it the ability to act turns a probabilistic component into an operational risk and blurs accountability.

## Forces

- Operators benefit most from explanation and preparation, not execution.
- Model errors are confident and plausible.
- Audit must remain unambiguous about who decided.

## Solution

Expose read operations only, plus at most a prepare operation returning a pre-filled workflow reference that a human then launches and another approves. Keep the assistant off the critical path so it can be disabled without operational consequence. Version agent definitions and prompts like any other rule.

## Trade-offs

The assistant cannot close the loop, which is the point. Value is measured in diagnosis time rather than in actions taken.

## When not to use this

In non-production environments with no client data and no service impact, write-capable tooling is legitimate and considerably more useful.

# PAT-009 — Dual-mode EPC/5GC progressive core migration

## Problem

A mission-critical mobile network must deliver MCX services continuously while migrating from a 4G EPC core to a 5G Standalone (SA) architecture. A hard cutover is operationally unacceptable: a failed migration at 02:00 means emergency calls fail.

## Forces

- MCX service continuity is non-negotiable during migration phases.
- Not all radio sites and devices will be 5G SA-capable simultaneously.
- The vendor's upgrade schedule and the programme's contractual delivery dates may not align.
- No migration test in a lab fully captures a live production system under load.

## Solution

Deploy a **dual-mode EPC/5GC core** from day one. Both EPC and 5GC NFs run concurrently in the same platform. MCX services attach through the mode appropriate to the device's RAN capability. The 5GC is activated progressively: first for new RAN sites, then for migrated sites, finally decommissioning the EPC only after a shadow validation period (`PAT-002`) demonstrates zero session loss.

Migration gates are enforced architecturally, not by policy alone:
- A device that registers on EPC cannot accidentally trigger a 5GC path.
- Rollback is a configuration change in the automation chain, not a physical operation.
- The MCX application layer is core-mode agnostic; it sees services, not NAS stacks.

## Trade-offs

Increases platform footprint and operational complexity during the migration window. Requires the compute platform to support both EPC and 5GC NFs simultaneously. Demands rigorous CMDB tracking of per-site core mode to avoid dual-registration anomalies.

## When not to use this

Where the programme timeline allows a greenfield deployment with no legacy EPC to migrate from — in that case, deploy 5G SA directly and avoid the dual-mode overhead.

## Seen in

National MCX systems (multi-lot programmes, 2025–2026) where contractual MCX service availability is committed before all RAN sites are 5G SA-ready.

# PAT-010 — Four-plane network separation (Service / Control / Management / OOB)

## Problem

A mission-critical platform that mixes user traffic, signalling, management, and break-glass operations on shared infrastructure creates compound failure modes: a DDoS on the service plane takes down the management plane; a misconfiguration pushed via the management plane can crash the service plane it is supposed to protect; a compromised management path gives an attacker visibility into live session state.

## Forces

- Regulatory frameworks (NIS2, SecNumCloud) require separation between operational and administrative planes.
- `P-009` (Independent Failure Domain): recovery and observability chains must share zero infrastructure with the systems they manage.
- Break-glass access must be available precisely when the main management path has failed.
- Network segmentation must be enforceable by infrastructure, not solely by policy.

## Solution

Enforce **four hermetically separated planes** across the platform:

| Plane | Function | Isolation Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Service** | User-facing application traffic (MCX, GIS, user data) | No management interface reachable from service addresses |
| **Control** | Signalling, session control, mobility, policy enforcement | Rate-limited; separated from user data at L3 minimum |
| **Management** | Configuration, provisioning, FCAPS, ITSM, automation southbound | Accessible only from the dedicated management network; PAM-gated |
| **Out-of-Band (OOB)** | Break-glass access, recovery tools, bastion hosts | Physically or cryptographically isolated; independent power and transport path |

Enforcement is architectural:
- VLAN separation is the minimum; physical separation for OOB and Management where threat model requires it.
- The automation engine's southbound path runs in the Management plane; its configuration state lives in Git (Service plane never touches the configuration store directly).
- The OOB bastion has no route to the Service plane; it can only reach management interfaces of infrastructure elements.

## Trade-offs

Increases network complexity and requires disciplined IPAM. Management-plane incidents (e.g. BGP misconfiguration on the management VRF) do not affect user traffic, but they do blind the NOC — operational runbooks must account for operating with reduced visibility.

## When not to use this

Small deployments where physical plane separation is impractical may implement logical separation (VRF + ACL) with a documented risk acceptance. Full four-plane physical separation is required for national PPDR systems and systems seeking SecNumCloud or equivalent qualification.

## Seen in

National mission-critical mobile networks (multi-site, 2025–2026). 3GPP architecture specifications implicitly assume this separation; ETSI NFV and O-RAN explicitly require it for operator plane isolation.

# PAT-011 — MCX SLA latency budget allocation

## Problem

An MCX system has a contractual end-to-end MCPTT access time target (typically < 1,000 ms E2E, < 300 ms in-cell). This budget must be distributed across RAN, core, transport, and the MCX application stack. Without explicit allocation, every team optimises locally, and the integration discovers the budget is overrun only during acceptance testing — where fixing it costs ten times more.

## Forces

- A latency budget assigned to no one is always exceeded.
- Each component owner (RAN, core, transport, MCX application) will negotiate their own share without a system-level referee.
- The budget is asymmetric: the in-cell target (< 300 ms) is tighter than the E2E target (< 1,000 ms) because it excludes transport and MCX server processing.
- Active probes must verify the budget continuously in production, not just at FAT/SAT.

## Solution

Establish a **normalised MCX SLA latency budget** at the start of the technical design phase and maintain it as a first-class architecture artefact throughout the programme.

### Reference SLA targets (3GPP / ETSI MCPTT baseline)

| Metric | Reference Value | Standard Reference |
|---|---|---|
| MCPTT access time (in-cell) | < 300 ms | 3GPP TS 22.179 |
| MCPTT access time (end-to-end) | < 1,000 ms | 3GPP TS 22.179 |
| Mouth-to-ear latency | < 300 ms | ITU-T P.340 |
| MCX late entry time | < 350 ms | 3GPP TS 22.179 |
| MCPTT listening quality | > 4.0 MOS | ITU-T P.800 |
| GIS moving-device update rate | ≤ 30 s or ≤ 200 m | Programme SLA |
| GIS display latency | ≤ 20 s | Programme SLA |

### Budget decomposition per component (illustrative — to be confirmed per engagement)

| Component | Budget allocation | Measurement point |
|---|---|---|
| UE processing + codec | 20–40 ms | UE instrumentation |
| RAN air interface + scheduler | 30–80 ms | RAN KPI export |
| Core network (EPC/5GC bearer setup) | 50–100 ms | Core NF trace |
| Transport (DC-to-DC, if remote MCX) | 5–20 ms | IP probe |
| MCX server processing (floor grant) | 50–100 ms | MCX application trace |
| Margin and jitter | 50 ms | — |
| **Total (in-cell scenario)** | **≤ 300 ms** | Active probe |

For E2E (dispatching position to field device), add the dispatcher leg: typically 100–200 ms additional.

### Enforcement

1. **Architecture gate**: the budget table is reviewed at PDR. Any component allocation exceeding its share requires explicit approval.
2. **Active probes in production**: synthetic MCPTT test calls (SIP test agent) run continuously and alert the NOC when the budget is at risk.
3. **Per-component KPI ownership**: each domain team owns and reports its contribution to the budget at the monthly architecture review.

## Trade-offs

Creates governance overhead during the design phase. Requires instrumentation at each component boundary (which is valuable anyway for operational observability). The budget is an engineering commitment, not a contractual guarantee — actual values depend on platform dimensioning and network topology.

## When not to use this

Do not apply a fixed budget to a system where the SLA is not contractually defined. In that case, use the 3GPP normative values as a design target but do not create governance gates around them.

## Seen in

National MCX programmes (2025–2026) with contractual MCPTT performance acceptance criteria.

# Claims register

One row per statement in the proposal that a customer could hold us to. Filled
before the proposal is reviewed, not after.

| # | Claim as written in the proposal | Section | Evidence level | Evidence | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | proven / designed / vendor-stated / aspirational | | keep / soften / drop / substantiate |

## Evidence levels

- **proven** — delivered and observed in a production engagement we can name.
- **designed** — designed and validated in a lab or a pre-production environment.
- **vendor-stated** — the vendor documents it; we have not verified it.
- **aspirational** — a target, a roadmap item, or a capability we intend to build.

## Rules

1. Any `aspirational` claim must be reworded as a trajectory ("the architecture
   supports progressing towards...") or dropped. It is never presented as a
   delivered capability.
2. Any `vendor-stated` claim that is load-bearing for the bid must have a
   questionnaire item attached, and the answer must arrive before signature.
3. The register is attached to the bid review pack. A proposal without one is
   not ready for review.

## Why this exists

Autonomous-operations proposals fail technical evaluation for over-claiming far
more often than for under-scoping. The register makes moderation a mechanical
step rather than an argument between the architect and the bid manager.

# Getting started

## 1. Publish it on GitHub

The repository is already initialized with one commit on `main`. Two ways to
push it to your account.

**With the GitHub CLI** (creates the remote repository and pushes in one step):

```bash
cd architecture-kb
gh auth login                       # once per machine
gh repo create <org-or-user>/architecture-kb \
    --private --source=. --remote=origin --push
```

**Without the CLI** — create an empty repository on github.com first (no README,
no .gitignore, no licence), then:

```bash
cd architecture-kb
git remote add origin git@github.com:<org-or-user>/architecture-kb.git
git push -u origin main
```

Use SSH (`git@github.com:`) rather than HTTPS if your organization requires it;
otherwise `https://github.com/<org-or-user>/architecture-kb.git` works with a
personal access token.

If the repository was initialized before you had `git` configured, set the
authorship on the first commit:

```bash
git config user.name  "Your Name"
git config user.email "you@company.com"
git commit --amend --reset-author --no-edit
git push -u origin main --force-with-lease   # only safe before anyone cloned
```

## 2. Protect the main branch

Do this before inviting anyone. On GitHub: **Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New
branch ruleset**, target `main`, and enable:

- Require a pull request before merging, with **1 approval**.
- Require review from **Code Owners** (this activates the `CODEOWNERS` file).
- Require status checks to pass: select the `validate` workflow.
- Block force pushes.

Without this, `CODEOWNERS` is decorative and the front-matter validation is
advisory. With it, the governance described in `GOVERNANCE.md` is enforced by
the platform rather than by goodwill.

Then replace the placeholder handles in `CODEOWNERS` with real GitHub usernames
or teams, and commit that as your second change — through a pull request, to
prove the flow works.

## 3. Onboard a colleague

```bash
git clone git@github.com:<org-or-user>/architecture-kb.git
cd architecture-kb
pip install pyyaml jsonschema
python schema/validate.py           # should print 0 errors
```

Then read `CONTRIBUTING.md`. It is two pages and it answers the only question a
new contributor has: *what goes where, and when.*

## 4. The everyday loop

```bash
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c adr/0014-transport-vendor-selection

# write the asset, copying the closest existing one rather than the template
cp decisions/ADR-0006.md decisions/ADR-0014.md
$EDITOR decisions/ADR-0014.md

python schema/validate.py
git add decisions/ADR-0014.md
git commit -m "ADR-0014: transport vendor selection"
git push -u origin adr/0014-transport-vendor-selection
gh pr create --fill                 # or open it in the web interface
```

Branch prefixes: `adr/`, `pat/`, `principle/`, `qst/`, `est/`, `risk/`, `view/`,
`project/<name>/`, `harvest/<engagement>-<phase>`.

Commit messages start with the asset identifier. That is the whole convention —
`git log --oneline decisions/` then reads as a decision history.

## 5. Keeping identifiers unique

Identifiers are allocated by taking the next free number **on `main`**, not on
your branch. Two people drafting `ADR-0014` simultaneously is the one collision
this base can suffer, and `python schema/validate.py` catches it at review time.
For a team larger than five, open the "Decision needed" issue first: the issue
number reserves the slot and gives the decision a place to be discussed before
it is written.

## 6. What good contribution looks like

The base fails in one of two ways, and both are avoidable.

**It fills with drafts nobody promoted.** Prevention: `draft` assets older than
two harvests are deleted, and CI warns you before that. Write fewer, finished
assets.

**It becomes an archive nobody trusts.** Prevention: the harvest. Create the
harvest issue at phase kickoff, not at phase end — an obligation that appears at
the end is an obligation that is skipped. The single most valuable contribution
anyone makes to this base is the `actuals` line in an estimate and the
`materialized_in` line in a risk register, because those are the two things no
amount of architecture thinking can produce.

## 7. Wiring the agents

Implement the server described in `mcp/SPEC.md` against a clone of this
repository, and give it read-only credentials. Agents draft through pull
requests and never push. When you add the server to your agent framework, add
the prompt fragment at the end of the specification: it is what makes an agent
state the confidence level of what it asserts instead of flattening your
assumptions into facts.

# Glossary

**Break-glass** — procedure allowing critical recovery actions when the
management platform itself is unavailable.

**Claims register** — bid artefact recording the evidence level behind every
statement made in a proposal.

**Closed loop** — chain from detection to remediation. *Supervised* when a human
approval gates the action.

**Continuous compliance evaluation** — automated, ongoing inspection of operational
posture against regulatory and architectural baselines to prevent compliance drift.

**Drift** — difference between the observed configuration of an asset and its
intended configuration.

**Early warning (24h)** — rapid formal notification mechanism triggering an initial
alert to national CSIRTs and stakeholders within 24 hours of detecting a significant incident.

**Essential entity / Important entity** — classification criteria under EU cybersecurity
regulations (NIS 2) defining the stringency of supervisory oversight and mandatory security baselines.

**Fallback plan** — pre-validated configuration applied to recover from a known
degraded condition; bound to the baseline it assumes.

**Harvest** — timeboxed end-of-phase session that returns field experience into
this base.

**Immutable audit log** — tamper-proof recording mechanism (such as WORM storage or
cryptographically signed audit trails) guaranteeing non-repudiation of administrative events.

**Northbound interface** — vendor-exposed management interface through which an
external system operates a domain without bypassing its element manager.

**Security baseline** — documented, version-controlled set of minimum cryptographic,
access, and configuration requirements that every deployed component must meet.

**Service plane / infrastructure plane** — the two observation planes: signals
contributing to a delivered service, and signals describing the hosting platform.

**Shadow environment** — isolated environment receiving duplicated production
telemetry, able to evaluate rules but not to act.

**Source of truth** — the system that holds the intended state; for
configuration, a version control repository.

**Sovereignty boundary** — architectural perimeter ensuring customer key autonomy,
strict EU data localization, and legal immunity against foreign extraterritorial disclosure orders.

**Supply chain security baseline** — mandatory verification of third-party software
provenance, signed Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), and strict vendor boundary enforcement.

# Knowledge server — specification

A read-only Model Context Protocol server over this repository, so that agents
consume **typed assets** rather than fragments of prose retrieved by similarity.

## Why not retrieval over the generated documents

Chunking a design dossier destroys the structure that gives the content meaning:
a principle separated from its verification clause, or a decision separated from
its rejected alternatives, reads as an assertion. An agent then recomposes
something plausible and wrong. Serving whole, typed assets with their metadata
avoids the failure mode entirely, and filtering on `phase` and `domain` is more
precise than semantic search over the same corpus.

## Tools

| Tool | Arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `list_assets` | `type`, `phase`, `domain`, `status` | Identifiers and titles matching the filter |
| `get_asset` | `id` | The full asset with its front matter |
| `search_assets` | `query`, filters | Whole assets ranked by relevance, never fragments |
| `get_principles_for` | `phase`, `domain` | Active principles with statement and verification clause |
| `get_decision_trail` | `id` | The decision plus what it supersedes and what superseded it |
| `list_open_questions` | `engagement` | Questionnaire items still unanswered in a project instance |
| `get_estimate` | `id`, `work_packages` | Range, variance drivers and any recorded actuals |
| `get_risks_for` | `domain`, `phase` | Register entries with mitigations and materialization history |
| `render_view` | `generator`, `parameters` | A rendered diagram from `views/generators` |
| `draft_asset` | `type`, `content` | A branch and pull request — **never a direct write** |

## Mandatory behaviours

- Only `status: active` assets are returned unless `status` is explicitly set.
- Every response carries the asset's `confidence` and `last_reviewed`. An agent
  that presents an `assumed` item as fact is misusing the base; prompt for it.
- `draft_asset` opens a pull request labelled `agent-drafted`. There is no write
  tool, no exception, and no service account with push rights to `main`.
- Assets under `projects/` are only served when the engagement is named
  explicitly, so that client material never leaks into a generic answer.

## Suggested agent prompt fragment

> Before answering an architecture question, call `get_principles_for` with the
> relevant phase and domain, and `get_decision_trail` for any decision you rely
> on. State the `confidence` of anything you assert. If the base contains no
> asset covering the question, say so and propose a `draft_asset` rather than
> inventing a position.

## 4. Gouvernance de Solution et Principes d'Architecture

### 4.1 Vision Architecturale et Principes Directeurs

L'architecture est gouvernée par les principes système suivants, issus de la base de connaissances :

- **`P-001` (GitOps Généralisé)** : L'ensemble de la configuration réseau, radio et plateforme est déclaratif, versionné dans Git et déployé exclusivement par des pipelines CI/CD automatisés.
- **`P-003` (Actions Unitaires Bornées)** : Les boucles d'automatisation opèrent avec un rayon d'impact borné et prévisible. En cas d'échec inattendu, l'exécution s'arrête proprement et escalade sans compensation hasardeuse.
- **`P-004` (Autonomie Progressive)** : L'autonomie opérationnelle est octroyée sur preuves mesurées en mode de validation miroir, jamais accordée par défaut non vérifié.
- **`P-007` (Respect de la Frontière Fournisseur)** : L'orchestration s'effectue strictement via les APIs northbound supportées par les fournisseurs, sans altération des composants propriétaires internes.
- **`P-009` (Domaine de Défaillance Indépendant)** : Les chaînes de récupération, sauvegarde et observabilité ne partagent aucune infrastructure avec les systèmes actifs qu'elles supervisent.
- **`P-010` (Un Maître par Domaine de Données)** : Un seul système maître autoritaire par domaine de données (CMDB pour l'inventaire, HSS/UDM pour les profils abonnés, SM-DP+ pour les eSIM).
- **`P-011` (Séparation des Plans d'Observation)** : Séparation hermétique entre la télémétrie d'infrastructure et les flux de signalisation applicatifs mission-critiques.
- **`P-015` (Le Modèle Reste dans le Périmètre de Confiance)** : Inférence locale souveraine ; aucune donnée, contexte ou métadonnée opérationnelle ne quitte le périmètre sécurisé du projet.

### 4.2 Principes de Gouvernance et de Sécurité

**Sécurité dès la conception (Security by Design)** : La sécurité n'est pas un ajout a posteriori mais une propriété fondatrice de l'architecture. Tous les composants sont conçus sécurisés dès leur spécification initiale.

**Protection de la vie privée dès la conception (Privacy by Design)** : Les données personnelles, de localisation et les enregistrements de communications sont protégés par des moyens architecturaux (isolation des tenants, RBAC, pseudonymisation, règles de rétention) et non uniquement par des processus.

**Gouvernance de la chaîne d'approvisionnement** : Les composants tiers font l'objet d'une analyse de composition logicielle (SCA), d'un suivi SBOM et d'une vérification des certifications fournisseurs avant intégration.

**Objectifs de gouvernance sécurité :**
- Maintenir une séparation stricte entre les plans administratif, opérationnel et données
- Appliquer le principe de moindre privilège à tous les profils opérationnels
- Assurer une production continue de preuves de conformité (automatisée, non périodique)
- Définir des lignes de défense explicites (L1 Prévention / L2 Détection / L3 Réponse)

## 7. Engagements de Qualité de Service et Déterminants Architecturaux

### 7.1 Attributs de Qualité Déterminant l'Architecture

|---|---|---|
| **Disponibilité** | Les services mission-critiques restent disponibles malgré les défaillances composant, accès et site | Hébergement géo-redondant, interfaces redondantes, conception HA, basculement automatique |
| **Résilience** | Dégradation contrôlée ; services essentiels préservés en conditions anormales | Voix MCPTT et localisation prioritaires sur la vidéo et les données non critiques |
| **Performance** | MCX, SIG, embarquement et flux opérationnels satisfont les cibles de latence et simultanéité mission-critiques | QoS, priorité/préemption, marge de capacité, sondes actives, supervision des SLA |
| **Sécurité** | Toutes les chaînes de service critiques authentifiées, autorisées, protégées, journalisées et supervisées | IAM, PAM, PKI, HSM/KMS, SecGW, SOC/SIEM, EDR, IDS, pistes d'audit |
| **Confidentialité** | Identité, localisation, CDR et données opérationnelles protégées selon le besoin d'en connaître | Isolation des tenants, RBAC, pseudonymisation, règles de rétention, auditabilité |
| **Interopérabilité** | Le système interopère avec les RAN, domaines externes, services gouvernementaux, EUCCS, futurs domaines MCX | Catalogue d'interfaces, passerelles de sécurité, IWF, protocoles normalisés |
| **Continuité opérationnelle** | NOC, SOC, ITSM assurent la détection, l'escalade, la restauration et le reporting en états dégradés | Procédures brise-glace, guides DR, tableaux de bord, processus opérationnels dédiés |

### 7.2 Instantané de Référence des Performances MCX

> Ces valeurs sont incluses comme entrées de référence architecturale. Elles confirment l'enveloppe d'échelle et de qualité de service que la solution doit supporter. Les calculs d'ingénierie détaillés et le dimensionnement de plateforme sont traités séparément.

| Temps d'entrée tardive MCX | < 350 ms | Sonde active |
| Qualité d'écoute MCPTT | > 4,0 MOS | Évaluation périodique |
| Taux de mise à jour de position (mobile) | ≤ 30 s ou ≤ 200 m de déplacement | Sonde SIG |
| Latence d'affichage SIG | ≤ 20 s après mesure de position | E2E |
| Rétention des enregistrements MCX | {{ RECORDING_RETENTION }} (ex. : 10 % des appels, 1 an) | Audit |
| Rétention des informations d'audit MCX | ≥ {{ AUDIT_RETENTION }} (ex. : 2 ans) | Conformité |
| RTO / RPO | Définis par classe de criticité de service (voir §{{ DR_SECTION }}) | Test DR |

**Hypothèses préliminaires et décisions ouvertes** — à affiner lors des revues PDR/CDR :
- L'architecture est dimensionnée pour la cible contractuelle ; la population opérationnelle à l'Acceptation Finale peut être inférieure
- Le trafic MCX est supposé dominé par la voix de groupe avec forte simultanéité et distribution asymétrique
- Les valeurs RTO/RPO ne sont pas fixées à ce stade ; elles sont définies par classe de criticité de service
- Les règles de rétention (historique SIG, CDR, enregistrements MCX, événements sécurité) seront confirmées avec les parties prenantes légales et sécurité

## 8. Architecture Logique de Solution et Frontières de Confiance

### 8.1 Vue d'Ensemble de l'Architecture Logique

Le système s'articule autour d'un ensemble de **domaines logiques** qui coopèrent pour délivrer les services mission-critiques. Chaque domaine possède un périmètre fonctionnel clairement défini, une frontière de responsabilité et un ensemble d'interfaces externes contrôlées.

### 8.3 Séparation des Plans Architecturaux

L'architecture logique applique une **séparation en quatre plans** pour éviter le couplage fonctionnel et clarifier les responsabilités :

| Plan | Fonction | Règle d'isolation |
|---|---|---|
| **Plan Service** | Trafic applicatif utilisateur (MCX, SIG, données) | Aucun accès direct depuis les interfaces de gestion |
| **Plan Contrôle** | Signalisation, contrôle de session, mobilité, politique | Séparé des données utilisateur ; limité en débit |
| **Plan Management** | Configuration, provisionnement, supervision, ITSM | Accessible uniquement depuis le réseau de gestion dédié |
| **Plan Hors-Bande (OOB)** | Brise-glace, récupération, accès bastion | Isolé physiquement ou logiquement ; alimentation et transport indépendants |

> *Règle architecturale :* Un chemin de gestion partageant calcul, réseau ou stockage avec le service qu'il gère viole `P-009` (Domaine de Défaillance Indépendant) et doit être rejeté.

## 14. Architecture Sécurité et Confidentialité

### 14.1 Vue d'Ensemble de la Posture Sécurité

Toutes les chaînes de service critiques sont **authentifiées, autorisées, protégées, journalisées et supervisées**. La posture sécurité est définie par cinq couches architecturales :

| Couche | Périmètre | Contrôles clés |
|---|---|---|
| **Périmètre** | Frontières externes, DMZ | Pare-feu, SecGW, IDS/IPS, atténuation DDoS |
| **Plateforme & Charges de travail** | Plateforme conteneurs, VMs, OS | Référentiels CIS, sécurité runtime, signature d'images |
| **Identité & Accès** | Tous les profils opérationnels | IAM, PAM, MFA, authentification par certificat |
| **Données & Cryptographie** | Données au repos, en transit, en usage | PKI, KMS, HSM (CC EAL4+), TLS 1.3 minimum |
| **Détection & Réponse** | Supervision continue | SOC, SIEM, EDR, CSIRT, gestion des vulnérabilités |

### 14.2 Principes de Sécurité et Architecture Zéro-Confiance

- **Moindre privilège** : chaque utilisateur, service et composant reçoit uniquement les permissions nécessaires à sa fonction
- **Supposer la compromission** : l'architecture suppose qu'une compromission du périmètre est possible ; le mouvement latéral doit être prévenu
- **Vérification explicite** : chaque demande d'accès authentifiée et autorisée, quelle que soit la source
- **Zéro privilège permanent** : les accès administrateurs sont accordés à la demande avec des sessions à durée limitée

**Zonage sécuritaire :**

| Zone | Contenu | Règle d'accès |
|---|---|---|
| Public / DMZ | Interfaces Internet, SecGW | Filtrage entrant strict |
| Service | MCX, SIG, charges applicatives | mTLS inter-service uniquement |
| Management | OSS/BSS, automatisation, NOC | Gestion via PAM, MFA obligatoire |
| Hors-bande | Brise-glace, récupération, bastion | Isolé physiquement / cryptographiquement |
| Tenant-N | Ressources dédiées à l'OU | Aucun accès inter-tenant par défaut |

## 4. Solution Governance and Architecture Principles

### 4.1 Architecture Vision and Guiding Principles

The architecture is governed by the following system-level principles, derived from the Knowledge Hub baseline:

- **`P-001` (Generalized GitOps)**: All network, radio, and platform configuration is declarative, version-controlled in Git, and deployed exclusively through automated CI/CD pipelines.
- **`P-003` (Bounded Unitary Actions)**: Closed automation loops operate with a bounded, predictable blast radius. On unexpected failure, execution halts cleanly and escalates without hazardous compensation.
- **`P-004` (Graduated Autonomy)**: Operational autonomy is earned through measured evidence in shadow validation mode, never granted as an unverified default.
- **`P-007` (Respect the Vendor Boundary)**: Orchestration interfaces strictly through vendor-supported northbound APIs without tampering with proprietary software internals.
- **`P-009` (Independent Failure Domain)**: Recovery, backup, and observability chains share zero infrastructure with the active systems they manage.
- **`P-010` (One Master per Data Domain)**: Exactly one authoritative master system per data domain (CMDB for inventory, HSS/UDM for subscriber profiles, SM-DP+ for eSIM).
- **`P-011` (Separate Observation Planes)**: Hermetic separation between platform infrastructure telemetry and mission-critical application signalling flows.
- **`P-015` (The Model Stays Inside the Trust Boundary)**: Sovereign local inference; no prompt, context, or operational metadata leaves the secure project boundary.

### 4.2 Governance and Security Principles

**Security by Design**: Security is not an add-on but a foundational property of the architecture. All components are designed to be secure from their initial specification.

**Privacy by Design**: Personal data, location data, and communication records are protected by architectural means (tenant isolation, RBAC, pseudonymisation, retention rules) rather than process alone.

**Supply Chain Governance**: Third-party components are subject to software composition analysis, SBOM tracking, and vendor certification verification prior to integration.

**Security governance objectives:**
- Maintain strict separation between administrative, operational, and data planes
- Enforce least-privilege access across all operational profiles
- Ensure continuous compliance evidence production (automated, not periodic)
- Define explicit lines of defence (L1 Prevention / L2 Detection / L3 Response)

## 8. Logical Solution Architecture and Trust Boundaries

### 8.1 Logical Architecture Overview

The system is structured around a set of **logical domains** that cooperate to deliver mission-critical services. Each domain has a clearly defined functional scope, ownership boundary, and set of controlled external interfaces.

*(See companion logical architecture diagram — consolidated end-to-end view)*

### 8.2 Logical Domain Models

| Logical Domain | Function | Mastered By |
|---|---|---|
| MCX Services Domain | Mission-critical application services (MCPTT, MCVideo, MCData, KMS) | {{ MCX_OWNER }} |
| Core Network Domain | Subscriber management, bearer, session, mobility | {{ CORE_OWNER }} |
| Transport & Underlay Domain | IP underlay, routing, synchronisation | {{ TRANSPORT_OWNER }} |
| Radio Access Domain | Radio bearers, spectrum management | {{ RAN_OWNER }} |
| Device & Fleet Domain | Terminal lifecycle, eSIM, MDM | {{ DEVICE_OWNER }} |
| GIS / COP Domain | Location, geospatial services, operational picture | {{ GIS_OWNER }} |
| Observation Domain | Telemetry, SIEM, service assurance, NOC | {{ OBS_OWNER }} |
| Automation Domain | GitOps, closed loops, configuration management | {{ AUTO_OWNER }} |
| Security Domain | IAM, PKI, KMS, HSM, SOC | {{ SEC_OWNER }} |
| Management Domain | OSS/BSS, CMDB, ITSM | {{ MGMT_OWNER }} |

### 8.3 Separation of Architectural Planes

The logical architecture enforces **four-plane separation** to avoid functional coupling and clarify responsibilities:

| Plane | Function | Isolation Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Service Plane** | User-facing application traffic (MCX, GIS, data) | No direct access from management interfaces |
| **Control Plane** | Signalling, session control, mobility, policy | Separated from user data; rate-limited |
| **Management Plane** | Configuration, provisioning, monitoring, ITSM | Accessible only from dedicated management network |
| **Out-of-Band (OOB) Plane** | Break-glass, recovery, bastion access | Physically or logically isolated; independent power and transport |

> *Architectural rule:* A management path that shares compute, network or storage with the service it manages violates `P-009` (Independent Failure Domain) and must be rejected.

### 8.4 Trust Boundaries

## 14. Security and Privacy Architecture

### 14.1 Security Posture Overview

All critical service chains are **authenticated, authorised, protected, logged and supervised**. The security posture is defined by five architectural layers:

| Layer | Scope | Key Controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Perimeter** | External boundaries, DMZ | Firewall, SecGW, IDS/IPS, DDoS mitigation |
| **Platform & Workload** | Container platform, VMs, OS | CIS benchmarks, runtime security, image signing |
| **Identity & Access** | All operational profiles | IAM, PAM, MFA, certificate-based auth |
| **Data & Cryptography** | Data at rest, in transit, in use | PKI, KMS, HSM (CC EAL4+), TLS 1.3 minimum |
| **Detection & Response** | Continuous monitoring | SOC, SIEM, EDR, CSIRT, vulnerability management |

### 14.2 Security Principles and Zero-Trust Architecture

- **Least privilege**: every user, service and component receives only the permissions required for its function
- **Assume breach**: architecture assumes perimeter compromise is possible; lateral movement must be prevented
- **Verify explicitly**: every access request authenticated and authorised, regardless of source location
- **Zero standing privileges**: administrative access granted on demand with time-bound sessions

**Security zoning:**

| Zone | Content | Access Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Public / DMZ | Internet-facing interfaces, SecGW | Strictly filtered inbound |
| Service | MCX, GIS, application workloads | Service-to-service mTLS only |
| Management | OSS/BSS, automation, NOC | PAM-gated, MFA mandatory |
| Out-of-Band | Break-glass, recovery, bastion | Physically / cryptographically isolated |
| Tenant-N | UO-specific resources | No cross-tenant access by default |
